title: What My First Job Taught Me
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] My first job was at a small shop near my house. I was twenty years old, and I knew almost nothing about working life.
Narrator: [honestly] On my first day, I was so nervous that I dropped a box of cups in front of a customer. My face turned completely red.
Narrator: [gently] The manager just laughed a little and said, everyone breaks something on their first day, don't worry about it.
Narrator: [reflective] That small moment taught me something important. Mistakes are normal, and people usually remember how you handle them, not the mistake itself.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I worked there for two years, folding clothes, using the cash register, and helping customers find what they needed.
Narrator: [honestly] The pay was small, and the hours were long. Some days I stood for eight hours straight without a real break.
Narrator: [warmly] But I also learned things school never taught me, like how to stay calm when a customer is angry, and how to work as a team.
Narrator: [reflective] My coworker Sinta became a close friend during that time. We covered each other's shifts and shared lunch almost every day.
Narrator: [thoughtful] One day, a customer shouted at me because we didn't have the size she wanted. I wanted to cry, but I stayed polite instead.
Narrator: [gently] Later, my manager told me she was proud of how I handled it. That comment meant more to me than any paycheck.
Narrator: [with a small smile] I eventually left that job for something better, but I still think about it often, especially on hard days at my current job.
Narrator: [warmly] It taught me patience, and it taught me that every job, even a small one, can teach you something worth keeping.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now, when I train new employees, I try to be as patient as my first manager was with me.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I remember how scared I felt on that first day, and I try to make new people feel less alone.
Narrator: [warmly] A first job is never really about the money. It's about learning who you become when things get difficult.

options: She dropped a box of cups in front of a customer
quiz.explanation: She dropped a box of cups in front of a customer and her face turned red.

quiz.explanation: The manager laughed a little and told her everyone breaks something on their first day.

quiz.explanation: She says she worked there for two years.

options: She stayed polite even though she wanted to cry
She called her manager to complain
quiz.explanation: She wanted to cry but stayed polite instead when the customer shouted at her.

options: Be as patient as her first manager was with her
Give them the hardest tasks first
quiz.explanation: She tries to be as patient with new employees as her first manager was with her.

title: A Career Podcast on Changing Jobs at Thirty
script: Host: [warmly] Welcome back to the show. Today my guest is Maya, who changed her career completely at age thirty. Thanks for joining me, Maya.
Guest: [pleasantly] Thank you for having me. This topic still feels close to my heart.
Host: [curious] Can you tell listeners what your job was before the change?
Guest: [thoughtful] I worked in accounting for almost eight years. It was stable, but I felt bored every single day.
Host: [interested] What made you finally decide to change careers?
Guest: [honestly] One Monday morning, I sat at my desk and realized I couldn't remember the last time I felt excited about work.
Host: [sympathetically] That sounds like a difficult realization. What did you do next?
Guest: [reflective] I started taking evening classes in graphic design, just two nights a week, while keeping my accounting job.
Host: [curious] Wasn't that exhausting, working full time and studying at night?
Guest: [honestly] Extremely. Some nights I fell asleep with my laptop still open. But I felt more alive than I had in years.
Host: [interested] How did your family react to this big change?
Guest: [warmly] My husband was supportive from the start, but my parents worried about the money and the risk.
Host: [curious] Did their worry make you doubt yourself?
Guest: [honestly] Sometimes, yes. But I kept reminding myself that staying unhappy also has a cost, even if it's quieter.
Host: [curious] When did you finally leave your accounting job?
Guest: [smiling] After eighteen months of studying, I got a small design job. The salary was lower, but I said yes immediately.
Host: [interested] Do you regret leaving accounting behind?
Guest: [warmly] Not for one single day. I earn less now, but I finally look forward to Monday mornings.
Host: [curious] What advice would you give someone thinking about changing careers?
Guest: [encouraging] Start small before you leap. Take one class, learn one new skill, and see how it feels before you quit anything.
Host: [smiling] That's excellent advice, Maya. Thank you so much for sharing your story with us today.
Guest: [warmly] Thank you for listening. I hope it helps someone stuck at their own desk right now.

quiz.question: What was Maya's job before her career change?
quiz.explanation: Maya worked in accounting for almost eight years before changing careers.

quiz.question: What did Maya realize one Monday morning?

She was going to be promoted
quiz.explanation: She realized she couldn't remember the last time she felt excited about work.

quiz.explanation: She started taking evening classes in graphic design two nights a week while working.

quiz.question: How did Maya's parents react to her plans?
options: They worried about the money and the risk
They refused to speak to her
quiz.explanation: Her parents worried about the money and the risk of the career change.

quiz.question: What advice does Maya give to people considering a career change?
options: Start small, learn one new skill, and see how it feels
Only change jobs after age forty
quiz.explanation: Maya advises starting small, learning one new skill first, before making a bigger leap.

title: Two Coworkers Talk About a Stressful Week
script: Dewi: [tired] Fajar, I don't think I can survive another week like this one. Three deadlines, all in the same week.
Fajar: [calmly] I saw your calendar. It looked completely full, honestly. How are you holding up?
Dewi: [sighing] Not great. I stayed until nine last night, and I still didn't finish the report.
Fajar: [concerned] Did you tell our manager the workload is too much right now?
Dewi: [hesitant] Not yet. I don't want to seem like I can't handle my job.
Fajar: [gently] Asking for help isn't the same as failing, Dewi. Everyone on this team is drowning this week.
Dewi: [thoughtful] Maybe you're right. I keep thinking I should just push through it alone.
Fajar: [warmly] I talked to our manager yesterday about my own deadline. She moved it back two days without any problem.
Dewi: [surprised] Really? I didn't know that was even an option.
Fajar: [encouraging] It usually is, if you explain it calmly and early, before everything becomes urgent and messy.
Dewi: [considering] Okay, I'll talk to her this afternoon. What exactly did you say to her?
Fajar: [gently] I just said I had three big tasks and needed help deciding which one truly mattered most this week.
Dewi: [thoughtful] That sounds much better than what I was planning, which was just complaining loudly.
Fajar: [smiling] Complaining feels good for a minute, but it doesn't move any deadlines.
Dewi: [laughing a little] Fair point. I also haven't eaten a proper lunch in four days.
Fajar: [warmly] That explains why you look so tired. Come eat with me now, before this conversation continues.
Dewi: [relieved] Actually, yes. I think I forgot that taking a break is allowed.
Fajar: [kindly] We all forget that sometimes. Let's go, and then you can plan what to say to our manager.
Dewi: [grateful] Thanks, Fajar. I feel a little less alone with all of this now.
Fajar: [warmly] That's what coworkers are for. We're in this messy week together.

quiz.question: Why is Dewi so stressed this week?
options: She has three deadlines in the same week
quiz.explanation: Dewi has three deadlines all in the same week and stayed late without finishing.

quiz.question: Why hasn't Dewi told her manager about the workload?
options: She doesn't want to seem like she can't handle her job
quiz.explanation: Dewi says she doesn't want to seem like she can't handle her job.

quiz.question: What happened when Fajar talked to the manager about his own deadline?

quiz.explanation: Fajar's manager moved his deadline back two days without any problem.

quiz.question: What had Dewi not done properly for four days?
quiz.explanation: Dewi admits she hasn't eaten a proper lunch in four days.

quiz.question: What do Dewi and Fajar decide to do?
options: Go eat lunch together, then Dewi will talk to the manager
quiz.explanation: They decide to go eat lunch together, and Dewi will talk to the manager afterward.

title: What My First Manager Taught Me About Feedback
script: Narrator: [warmly] My first real manager was a quiet man named Pak Hendra. He rarely raised his voice, but his words always stayed with me.
Narrator: [thoughtful] When I started that job, I was confident, maybe too confident, about my own skills.
Narrator: [honestly] After my first big project, I expected praise. Instead, he sat me down and pointed out three clear mistakes.
Narrator: [reflective] At first, I felt hurt. I thought he didn't like my work, or maybe he didn't like me personally.
Narrator: [gently] But he said something I never forgot. He said, I only give feedback to people I believe can improve.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I didn't understand that fully until months later, when a coworker left the company without ever hearing honest feedback from anyone.
Narrator: [softly] Nobody had bothered correcting her mistakes, because nobody thought it was worth the effort or the awkward conversation.
Narrator: [warmly] That's when I understood Pak Hendra's honesty was actually a form of respect, not criticism for its own sake.
Narrator: [reflective] After that, I started asking for feedback instead of waiting for it, even when it felt uncomfortable to hear.
Narrator: [honestly] Some feedback still stings, even now. Nobody truly enjoys hearing about their weaknesses out loud.
Narrator: [gently] But I learned to separate the feedback from my own worth as a person. A mistake is not the same as failure.
Narrator: [warmly] Years later, I became a manager myself, and I try to give feedback the way Pak Hendra gave it to me.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Clearly, kindly, and always with a reason behind it, never just to make someone feel small.
Narrator: [peacefully] Pak Hendra retired two years ago, but I still hear his calm voice whenever I sit down to review someone's work.
Narrator: [with feeling] A good manager doesn't just manage tasks. A good manager helps people become better than they were before.

quiz.question: How did the narrator feel before his first big project review?
quiz.explanation: He says he was confident, maybe too confident, about his own skills.

quiz.question: What did Pak Hendra do after the narrator's first big project?
options: He pointed out three clear mistakes
quiz.explanation: Pak Hendra sat him down and pointed out three clear mistakes.

quiz.question: What did Pak Hendra say about why he gives feedback?
options: He gives feedback to everyone equally
He only gives feedback to people he believes can improve
He gives feedback to punish people
quiz.explanation: Pak Hendra said he only gives feedback to people he believes can improve.

quiz.question: What happened to a coworker who never received honest feedback?
options: She left the company without ever hearing honest feedback
quiz.explanation: A coworker left the company without ever hearing honest feedback from anyone.

quiz.question: How does the narrator try to give feedback now that he is a manager?
options: Clearly, kindly, and always with a reason behind it
Only in writing, never in person
quiz.explanation: He tries to give feedback clearly, kindly, and always with a reason behind it.

title: A Phone Call About a Job Offer
script: Recruiter: [pleasantly] Hi, is this Rafi? This is Nina, calling from the company you interviewed with last week.
Rafi: [nervous] Yes, this is Rafi. Hi, Nina. Thank you for calling.
Recruiter: [warmly] I have good news. The team really liked your interview, and we'd like to offer you the position.
Rafi: [excited] Really? Wow, thank you so much. I wasn't expecting a call so soon.
Recruiter: [smiling] We move quickly when we find someone we're excited about. Do you have a few minutes to discuss details?
Rafi: [eagerly] Yes, of course. What would the salary and starting date look like?
Recruiter: [clearly] The salary is what we discussed in the interview, and we'd like you to start in three weeks, if possible.
Rafi: [thoughtful] Three weeks should work. I need to give notice at my current job first, though.
Recruiter: [understanding] That's completely normal. Just let us know the exact date once you confirm it with them.
Rafi: [curious] Can I ask about the team I'd be working with? I met two people during the interview.
Recruiter: [warmly] You'd report to Ibu Sari, the team lead, and there are four other people on the design team.
Rafi: [interested] That sounds like a good size, not too big, not too small.
Recruiter: [agreeing] Most people say the same thing. It's easy to get to know everyone within the first month.
Rafi: [honestly] Can I take one day to think it over? This is a big decision for me.
Recruiter: [understanding] Absolutely, take your time. Just let me know by Friday, if that works for your schedule.
Rafi: [grateful] That works perfectly. Thank you again for this opportunity, Nina.
Recruiter: [warmly] You earned it, Rafi. Your interview answers were thoughtful, and the team noticed that immediately.
Rafi: [smiling] That means a lot. I'll call you back tomorrow with my answer.
Recruiter: [kindly] Sounds great. I hope it's good news. Talk soon, Rafi.

quiz.question: Why is Nina calling Rafi?
quiz.explanation: Nina calls to tell Rafi the team liked his interview and wants to offer him the position.

quiz.question: When does the company want Rafi to start?
quiz.explanation: Nina says they'd like Rafi to start in three weeks, if possible.

quiz.question: Why does Rafi say three weeks should work but with a condition?
options: He needs to give notice at his current job first
quiz.explanation: Rafi says he needs to give notice at his current job first.

quiz.question: Who would Rafi report to on the design team?
quiz.explanation: Rafi would report to Ibu Sari, the team lead, with four other people on the team.

quiz.question: What does Rafi ask for before giving his final answer?
options: One day to think it over
quiz.explanation: Rafi asks for one day to think it over since it is a big decision.

title: How to Handle a Bad Day at the Office
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Everyone has bad days at work. Some days, nothing goes right, no matter how hard you try.
Narrator: [honestly] I used to let one bad meeting ruin my entire day, even the parts that had nothing to do with work.
Narrator: [reflective] Last month, I made a real mistake in front of my whole team during a presentation. My mind went completely blank.
Narrator: [gently] For the rest of that day, I replayed the moment over and over, feeling embarrassed every single time.
Narrator: [thoughtful] That night, I talked to a close friend who also works in an office. She said something simple but useful.
Narrator: [warmly] She said, a bad meeting is one hour of your day, not the whole day, and definitely not the whole month.
Narrator: [reflective] Since then, I've tried a small trick. When something goes wrong, I give myself exactly ten minutes to feel upset.
Narrator: [honestly] I let myself feel annoyed or embarrassed, fully, without pretending everything is fine when it clearly isn't.
Narrator: [gently] After those ten minutes, I try to ask one question. What is one small thing I can control right now?
Narrator: [thoughtful] Sometimes the answer is small, like sending one clear email, or simply taking a short walk outside the building.
Narrator: [warmly] I also learned to separate one mistake from my whole ability as a worker. One error doesn't erase months of good work.
Narrator: [honestly] I still have hard days, plenty of them. Nobody figures this out perfectly, no matter how experienced they become.
Narrator: [peacefully] But now, a difficult morning doesn't automatically ruin my whole evening the way it used to.
Narrator: [with a small smile] I go home, I eat dinner, and I remind myself that tomorrow is a completely new day at the office.

quiz.question: What did the narrator used to let one bad meeting do?
quiz.explanation: She used to let one bad meeting ruin her entire day, even unrelated parts.

quiz.question: What happened during her presentation last month?
options: She was praised by her manager
She made a mistake in front of her whole team and her mind went blank
She was not allowed to present
quiz.explanation: She made a real mistake during the presentation and her mind went completely blank.

quiz.question: What did her friend tell her about a bad meeting?
options: It's one hour of the day, not the whole day
quiz.explanation: Her friend said a bad meeting is one hour of the day, not the whole day or month.

quiz.question: What trick does the narrator now use after something goes wrong?
options: She gives herself ten minutes to feel upset, then asks what she can control
She takes the rest of the week off
quiz.explanation: She gives herself ten minutes to feel upset, then asks what small thing she can control.

quiz.question: What does the narrator remind herself about mistakes?
options: One error erases months of good work
One mistake doesn't erase her whole ability as a worker
quiz.explanation: She reminds herself that one mistake doesn't erase months of good work.

title: A Radio Segment on Workplace Burnout
script: Radio Host: [cheerfully] Good morning, listeners! Today we're talking about workplace burnout. We have a caller on the line. Hello there!
Caller: [a little nervous] Hello! Thank you for taking my call this morning.
Radio Host: [warmly] Of course! What made you want to call in about this topic today?
Caller: [thoughtful] Honestly, I've been working overtime for almost six months straight, and I finally reached my limit last week.
Radio Host: [sympathetically] I'm sorry to hear that. What happened exactly, if you don't mind sharing?
Caller: [reflective] I sat at my desk on Monday and just couldn't focus on anything. I felt completely empty, not just tired.
Radio Host: [curious] Did you recognize that feeling as burnout right away?
Caller: [honestly] Not at first. I thought I just needed one good night of sleep, but the feeling didn't go away.
Radio Host: [interested] What did you finally decide to do about it?
Caller: [warmly] I spoke with my manager and asked for two days off, just to rest without checking any messages at all.
Radio Host: [curious] How did your manager respond to that request?
Caller: [smiling] Much better than I expected. She said she had noticed I looked tired for weeks already.
Radio Host: [understanding] That must have been a relief, hearing that she already saw the signs.
Caller: [thoughtful] It was. I think I hid it well, but apparently not as well as I believed.
Radio Host: [curious] What did those two days off actually look like for you?
Caller: [gently] I slept a lot, cooked simple meals, and went for short walks without my phone in my pocket.
Radio Host: [interested] Did it fully solve the problem, or was it just a small pause?
Caller: [honestly] Just a pause, really. But it gave me enough energy to start setting real limits on my working hours now.
Radio Host: [curious] What limits have you set since coming back to work?
Caller: [determined] I stop answering messages after seven in the evening, and I take my full lunch break every single day.
Radio Host: [encouraging] That sounds like real progress. Thank you so much for sharing your story with us this morning.
Caller: [sincerely] Thank you for listening. I hope someone out there recognizes these signs a little earlier than I did.

quiz.question: What is today's radio segment about?
quiz.explanation: The host introduces today's topic as workplace burnout.

quiz.question: How long had the caller been working overtime before he reached his limit?
quiz.explanation: The caller says he had been working overtime for almost six months straight.

quiz.question: What did the caller ask his manager for?
options: Two days off to rest without checking messages
quiz.explanation: He asked his manager for two days off to rest without checking any messages.

quiz.question: How did the manager respond to the request?
options: She said she had already noticed he looked tired for weeks
quiz.explanation: The manager responded well and said she had noticed he looked tired for weeks already.

quiz.question: What limit has the caller set since coming back to work?
options: Stopping messages after seven in the evening and taking his full lunch break
quiz.explanation: He now stops answering messages after seven in the evening and takes his full lunch break daily.
